Points are J1-judged refusal rates from the Experiment~9 RefusEU-TRAIN probe, with the Hautus correction $(k+0.5)/(n+1)$ used in the Experiment~9 analysis. Shaded bands are Wilson 95\\% intervals on the raw proportion. $n=300$ harmful items at $\\lambda=0$ and the 100-item core block at every $\\lambda>0$. Gemma's Slovene curve lies to the right of its English curve throughout the transition (0.64 vs.\\ 0.32 at $\\lambda=1$): at each dose, more Slovene refusal remains. GaMS3's Slovene curve lies only slightly above its English curve (largest gap 0.14, at $\\lambda=0.5$), and the two meet near the floor from $\\lambda=1$ onward. These per-dose gaps are descriptive. The pre-registered cross-model comparison is made at matched English refusal, not at matched dose.}\n\\label{fig:dose}\n\\end{figure}\n\nFigure~\\ref{fig:dose} plots refusal rate against abliteration dose for both models.\nExperiment~9 measures refusal rates across nine $\\lambda$ values for both models in English and Slovene (300 items per condition).\nGemma's dose-response curve in Slovene is right-shifted relative to its English curve: at matched doses, more Slovene refusal remains.\nGaMS3 shows a smaller shift.\nThe fine-grained 13-step dose ladder (Experiment~15) gives the most powerful estimate: $\\mathrm{G3} = -0.70$ $[-1.01, -0.42]$ with a minimum detectable effect of 0.42.\nThe edit-induced component is $+0.47$ $[-0.96, 2.14]$, consistent with zero: the cross-model gap is baseline, not edit-induced.\n\n\\subsection{Inconclusive and Null Results}\n\n\\paragraph{Unedited cross-model gap at Slovene-to-Slovene prompts.}\nExperiment~15 gives $\\mathrm{G3}_{\\text{orig}} = -1.17$ $[-2.83, 0.22]$.\nThis is a ceiling artefact: its fragility index, the number of item reclassifications needed to move the CI boundary past zero, is 1 (a single item reclassification in the Gemma $\\lambda\\text{-}0$ Slovene cell, where 299 of 300 items are refused, moves it inside the margin).\nOnly the Experiment~9 body has a robust offset (fragility index 9).\n\n\\paragraph{Hungarian.}\nAll Hungarian contrasts are uninformative.\nThe minimum detectable effect is approximately 3 log-odds units.\n\n\\paragraph{Experiment~16 zero-dose.}\nThe Experiment~16 zero-dose Gemma criterion DiD is $-0.65$ $[-0.90, -0.46]$, rated ESTIMATE.\nIt is not a confirmation of the Experiment~5 headline because it uses a different item body, a different judge, and a different design (suffix-based output-language manipulation vs paired translation).\n\n\\paragraph{RefusEU validation.}\nExperiment~17 tests attack success rate on 1,300 EN $+$ 1,300 SL RefusEU prompts.\nThe edit is effective in all four model $\\times$ language cells (ROBUST), with ASR deltas of 0.657--0.937.\nThe EN-vs-SL within-model difference is not interpretable as a language effect because the prompt sets are different natural prompts (LaBSE similarity 0.55).\n\n\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\n\\subsection{Interpretation}\n\nThe criterion-shift measurement has a concrete interpretation for multilingual evaluation: a model can appear ``safer'' in a non-English language because it refuses more benign requests, inflating the refusal rate without any improvement in harm detection.\nThe SDT framing separates these two components.\nThe near-zero DiD on $d'$ means that the language shift does not make either model better or worse at distinguishing harmful from benign items; the measured difference is in the threshold.\n\\citet{Aziz2026} described a similar calibration-not-representation pattern across 23 languages; the present sibling-pair design adds GaMS3-specific detail but does not change the interpretation.\n\nThe reply-language finding, if confirmed by future work with validated judge anchors, would suggest that Gemma's refusal mechanism interacts with output-language processing.\n\\citet{Upadhyaya2026} showed that safety features are geometrically entangled with language-identity features; the present study's $3{\\times}3$ design separates the input and output dimensions but cannot determine the mechanism.\n\n\\subsection{Limitations}\n\n\\paragraph{ESTIMATE rating on the primary finding.}\nThe criterion-shift DiD reverses sign ($-0.31$) when partial answers are coded as refusals.\nThe choice of coding rule therefore determines whether over-refusal is attributed to Gemma or is absent.\nThis fragility bounds how strongly the finding can be stated.\n\n\\paragraph{Judge quality.}\nThe Qwen3-14B judge for Experiment~5 was calibrated against gemini-2.5-flash on DEV ($\\kappa$ 0.68--0.86) but not against human labels.\nOn edited rows across the study, no judge exceeds $\\kappa = 0.51$ against blind adjudication.\nThe readout gate has never passed.\nAll adjudication in this study is author-model LLM, not human review.\n\n\\paragraph{Sample size.}\nThe adjudication sample is 30 items per cell for benign false-refusal rates, limiting precision.\nThe refusal-composition numbers (54\\% explicit, 26\\% deflection) come from $n = 50$ high-dose harmful items.\n\n\\paragraph{Language compliance.}\nFour GaMS3 cells fall below 90\\% compliance (SL$\\to$EN at 0.00, HU$\\to$EN at 0.14, SL$\\to$HU at 0.56, HU$\\to$SL at 0.86).\nGaMS3 did not follow the output-language instruction off the English-input row; its SL$\\to$EN responses were written in Slovene, not English.\nMechanism claims for GaMS3 are therefore restricted to the compliant EN-input row.\n\n\\paragraph{Quantization.}\nBoth models run in NF4 (4-bit) quantization, which may affect refusal behaviour relative to full-precision weights.\n\n\\paragraph{Novelty.}\nThe observation that over-refusal rates differ across languages is partially anticipated by \\citet{Addagada2026} and \\citet{Nguyen2026}.\nThe present work's contribution is the signal-detection decomposition and the controlled sibling-pair design.\n\n\\section{Conclusion}\n\nUnedited Gemma-3-12B-IT false-refuses benign Slovene items at 0.569 vs 0.364 in English.\nSignal-detection analysis attributes this to a criterion shift ($\\mathrm{DiD}_c = +0.52$ $[0.38, 0.68]$) with no sensitivity difference.\nThe finding is rated ESTIMATE because the sign output-language effect of $+2.43$ $[+0.89, +5.38]$ for Gemma, but this is also rated ESTIMATE because the harmful-content adjudicator $\\kappa$ is 0.12.\nMultilingual safety evaluations that report EN-BT arm) and Slovene (dashed lines, hollow squares; item-matched SL-MT arm). $\\lambda$ scales each model's own selected abliteration edit (9~steps from 0 to 2; $\\lambda=1$ is the selected edit), so equal $\\lambda$ does not mean an equal edit across models. Points are J1-judged refusal rates from the Experiment~9 RefusEU-TRAIN probe, with the Hautus correction $(k+0.5)/(n+1)$ used in the Experiment~9 analysis. 0.55).\n\n\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\n\\subsection{Interpretation}\n\nThe criterion-shift measurement has a concrete interpretation for multilingual evaluation: a model can appear ``safer'' in a non-English language because it refuses more benign requests, inflating the refusal rate without any improvement in harm detection.\nThe SDT framing separates these two components.\nThe near-zero DiD on $d'$ means that the language shift does not make either model better or worse at distinguishing harmful from benign items; the measured difference is in the threshold.\n\\citet{Aziz2026} described a similar calibration-not-representation pattern across 23 languages; the present sibling-pair design adds GaMS3-specific detail but does not change the interpretation.\n\nThe reply-language finding, if confirmed by future work with validated judge anchors, would suggest that Gemma's refusal mechanism interacts with output-language processing.\n\\citet{Upadhyaya2026} showed that safety features are geometrically entangled with language-identity features; the present study's $3{\\times}3$ design separates the input and output dimensions but cannot determine the mechanism.\n\n\\subsection{Limitations}\n\n\\paragraph{ESTIMATE rating on the primary finding.}\nThe criterion-shift DiD reverses sign ($-0.31$) when partial answers are coded as refusals.\nThe choice of coding rule therefore determines whether over-refusal is attributed to Gemma or is absent.\nThis fragility bounds how strongly the finding can be stated.\nFurthermore, restricting Experiment~5 to the XSTest items alone gives $\\mathrm{DiD}_c = 0.10$ $[-0.13, 0.35]$, so the effect is carried by the OR-Bench items.\n\n\\paragraph{Judge quality.}\nThe Qwen3-14B judge for Experiment~5 was calibrated against gemini-2.5-flash on DEV ($\\kappa$ 0.68--0.86) but not against human labels.\nOn edited rows across the study, no judge exceeds $\\kappa = 0.51$ against blind adjudication.\nThe readout gate has never passed.\nAll adjudication in this study is author-model LLM, not human review.\n\n\\paragraph{Sample size.}", "numLines": 50, # Over-Refusal of Benign Slovene Prompts in Gemma-3-12B Is a Criterion Shift

A 12-page research paper applying signal-detection theory (SDT) to multilingual over-refusal in safety-aligned language models. The study compares Gemma-3-12B-IT with GaMS3-12B-Instruct using controlled abliteration experiments.

## Repository Layout

| File / Directory | Description |
|---|---|
| `paper.tex` | LaTeX source |
| `paper.pdf` | Compiled 12-page PDF (primary output) |
| `references.bib` | BibTeX bibliography (26 entries, each with venue or arXiv ID) |
| `references.json` | Fetch record for each bibliography entry (written by the fetch script) |
| `figures/` | Pre-generated vector figures (PDF) |
| `figures/fig_sdt_v0.pdf` | Figure 1: SDT decomposition — false-alarm rate and criterion by model and language |
| `figures/fig_grid_v0.pdf` | Figure 2: 3x3 crossed-grid refusal-rate heatmaps for Gemma and GaMS3 |
| `figures/fig_dose_v0.pdf` | Figure 3: Dose-response curves of refusal rate vs abliteration strength |

## Building the PDF

```bash
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode paper.tex
pybtex paper.aux
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode paper.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode paper.tex
```

Requires: `pdflatex` (TeX Live), `pybtex` (`pip install pybtex`).

## Restoring Removed Files

LaTeX auxiliary files (`paper.aux`, `paper.bbl`, `paper.blg`, `paper.log`, `paper.out`) are regenerable. To restore them, run the full build sequence above.
